KEY MESSAGE 1...Rain moves through the area today, though 
drought relief is unlikely.

KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...
A cold front continues to push southeast towards our forecast
area, though remains west of the Saint Lawrence River Valley as
of 3 AM this morning. The front should push through the northern
half of the forecast area by late morning, then through the
Downeast region through this afternoon and early evening hours.
This timing has slowed down with recent model runs, and the
front may continue to slow down to a crawl through the state,
leading to a slow exit this evening off the coast. Forecast rain
totals today remain below a quarter of an inch, with many areas
receiving less than a tenth of an inch. The catch is that should
a coastal low begin to develop along the front as it approaches
the Downeast coast, this could locally enhance rainfall amounts.
Overall, there will be little if any impact on the ongoing 
D1-D3 drought conditions. 

Additionally, a 700 mb shortwave will follow behind this front
tonight, and could lead to lingering rain showers, particularly
in the north, through the overnight hours. However, not much
additional rainfall is anticipated from this feature.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Widespread frost is expected for northern areas,
with patchy frost elsewhere for the Bangor region and interior
Downeast.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...
High pressure builds in behind the cold front Saturday, and,
with clearing clouds, will lead to temperatures falling well below
freezing overnight for northern areas. Temperatures will fall 
into the low to mid 30s for central areas, with lows in the low 
40s for near coastal areas. This could provide the first frost 
of the season for some areas in the Bangor region and interior 
Downeast. There is some uncertainty, however, of how far south 
the frost could get. The exact position of the high pressure, 
any coastal breezes, and any high cirrus clouds could all 
influence the extent of frost. Regardless, people should be 
prepared to protect any vulnerable vegetation across the area, 
especially if they are in lower lying areas that typically get 
colder. The frost/freeze program has ended for all counties
except Hancock and Washington counties, so frost headlines would
not be issued for Penobscot, Piscataquis, northern Somerset, or
Aroostook counties. Coastal Downeast should stay warm enough to
limit any frost, though check the forecast for updates. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...Another round of rain is possible Monday followed
by gusty westerly winds on Tuesday.

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...
Sunday night a cold surface high pressure that will have 
brought widespread frost Sunday AM shifts to the east over the
Maritimes. A potent vertically stacked low pressure system
tracks into north-central Quebec with a trailing potent cold
front. That front will swing across the CWA on Monday at the 
same time as a low pressure exits off the Mid-Atlantic coast. 
The interaction between the high pressure and the two lows 
provides significant uncertainty about rainfall. A few scenarios
are currently playing out in the ensemble models. 1. The high
pressure could dominate forcing the lows to stay to the north 
and south, limiting precip. 2. The Canadian low could enhance 
the coastal low as it rides the coast north, bringing more 
substantial precip to coastal areas. 3. The Canadian low could 
dominate, bringing enhanced precipitation along its cold front 
from the moisture over the southeast low. At this time, 
uncertainty from the models is high, so forecast confidence is 
low, with a wide range of precipitation values. 

Increasing confidence that Tuesday, as the low pressure system
deepens in the Northern Maritimes, we can expect strong surface
high pressure to dive over the eastern Great Lakes. This will lead to a
strong pressure gradient between the low and high resulting in
gusty W-WNW winds developing in the morning and peaking midday.
Probabilities for 35+ mph wind gusts have increased to 70-90%
with 40+ mph probabilities now 40-60%, mainly for Millinocket 
and areas north. There is ensemble guidance suggesting a 
potential of wind headlines but still uncertainty exists on 
exact expected wind speeds/gusts. However, it is likely that 
significant leaf loss may be possible in areas of Northern Maine
where peak foliage has been reached. Additional leaf loss 
possible in the Central Highlands to Downeast Maine where the 
foliage is moderate to high. Continue to monitor the forecast 
for updates, as models begin to get a better handle on the 
atmospheric set up.
